subject: physics
question_text: What is a Venturi meter? Explain how it is used.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 10 Short Answer Question 7 (printed p.109), printed again word for word as Long Answer Question 4 (printed p.112). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The 8-mark and 4-mark splits are both INVENTED and are a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms them. Physics hand-checked: continuity (A₁v₁ = A₂v₂) makes the fluid speed up in the narrower throat, and Bernoulli's principle — P/ρ + ½v² + gh = constant per unit mass, equivalently P + ½ρv² = constant per unit volume on a horizontal tube — then gives a lower pressure there; eliminating v₂ gives v₁ = √(2(P₁ − P₂) / ρ((A₁/A₂)² − 1)), matching the formula printed in the source book's answer.

cuts.label: Long answer — 8 marks
cuts.note: The full question as the paper asks it: what it is, its construction, the continuity-Bernoulli derivation, the manometer reading and its uses. The 8-mark split is a claim.

cuts.label: Short answer — 4 marks

s3_continuity.label: Continuity and Bernoulli
lines: By the equation of continuity A₁v₁ =
A₂v₂, the fluid speeds up in the narrow
throat, since A₂ is smaller than A₁.
By Bernoulli's principle, this rise in
speed is matched by a fall in pressure
at the throat.
s3_continuity.margin_note: Second mark. Say both laws, continuity gives the higher speed, Bernoulli gives the lower pressure, at the throat.
s3_continuity.why: These two laws together are the whole working principle: one fixes the speed change, the other turns it into a pressure change a manometer can read.
s3_continuity.memory_tip: Narrow throat: continuity speeds it up, Bernoulli drops the pressure.

lines: A manometer between the wide section and
the throat measures the pressure
difference P₁ − P₂. From it, the speed
is found:
s6_derive_speed.margin_note: Third mark. State how the manometer gives P₁ − P₂, then write the boxed formula for v₁.
s6_derive_speed.why: The manometer is what actually lets a reading of P₁ − P₂ be taken, and the boxed formula is what turns that reading into a speed.
s6_derive_speed.memory_tip: Read P₁ − P₂ on the manometer, then use the boxed formula for v₁.

s8_uses.margin_note: Fourth mark. Name flow-rate measurement, and at least one other device using the same principle.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: What a Venturi meter is
lines: A tube inserted into a pipe to measure
the speed of a flowing fluid.
It has a wide section, a narrow throat,
and widens again. It works on
Bernoulli's principle.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Name the device and say what it measures.
steps.why: Naming the device and its purpose first tells the reader what every later step is building towards.
common_mistakes: Describing it only as a kind of pipe, without saying what it measures.
Leaving out that it has a narrow throat between two wide sections.

recall.must_convey: That a Venturi meter is a tube with a constriction, fitted into a pipe to measure the speed of a flowing fluid, based on Bernoulli's principle.

a tube with a narrow throat in a pipe
it works on Bernoulli's principle

steps.memory_tip: Venturi meter: a tube with a pinch in the middle, reading fluid speed.

steps.label: Construction
lines: A short tube with a wide section of area
A₁ at each end, joined by a narrower
throat of area A₂ in the middle.
It is fitted into the pipe so the fluid
flows straight through it.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Name the three parts, wide, narrow throat, wide again, and their areas A₁ and A₂.
steps.why: The two areas A₁ and A₂ are the quantities every later formula in this answer is written in terms of.
common_mistakes: Not naming the areas A₁ and A₂ with symbols.
Describing a bend or a valve instead of a smooth narrowing.

recall.must_convey: That the meter is a wide-narrow-wide tube, area A₁ at the wide ends and A₂ at the throat, fitted into the pipe.

steps.memory_tip: Wide, narrow, wide: A₁, A₂, A₁ again.

steps.label: Continuity equation
lines: The volume of liquid flowing per second
is the same at every section of the
tube, since mass is conserved:
Since the throat area A₂ is smaller than
A₁, the throat speed v₂ is larger than
v₁. The fluid speeds up in the throat.
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Write A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ and say the fluid speeds up because A₂ is smaller.
steps.why: This is the first of the two laws that make the meter work: a smaller area forces a larger speed, whatever the pressure does.
common_mistakes: Saying only that the fluid speeds up, without saying WHY, the throat area is smaller.
Confusing which area is smaller. A₂, the throat, is smaller than A₁.

recall.must_convey: That by the equation of continuity A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, the fluid speeds up in the narrower throat.

steps.memory_tip: Narrower throat, faster flow: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.

steps.label: Bernoulli's principle
lines: For steady, non-viscous, incompressible
flow, the total energy per unit mass is
the same everywhere on a streamline:
For a horizontal tube, where h is the
same on both sides, the equivalent
per-unit-volume form is more convenient:
So where the speed v is larger, the
pressure P is smaller.
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. State the per-unit-mass relation, then the per-unit-volume form used for a horizontal tube.
steps.why: This is the second law: continuity fixed the speed change, and Bernoulli is what turns that speed change into a pressure change a manometer can actually read.
common_mistakes: Writing the per-unit-volume form as if it were the only form, without the per-unit-mass relation.
Forgetting that this simplified form needs a horizontal tube, so the gh terms cancel.

recall.must_convey: That by Bernoulli's principle, P + half rho v squared is constant on a horizontal tube, so a larger speed means a smaller pressure.

steps.label: Pressure difference
lines: Put v₂ = (A₁/A₂) v₁ from continuity into
the Bernoulli relation P + ½ρv² =
constant and simplify:
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. Substitute v₂ from continuity into the Bernoulli relation and simplify.
steps.why: Eliminating v₂ leaves a relation between the pressure difference and v₁ alone, which is the quantity the meter is actually built to measure.
common_mistakes: Substituting v₁ for v₂ instead of v₂ for v₁.
Dropping the square on the area ratio (A₁/A₂).

recall.must_convey: That substituting v₂ = (A₁/A₂)v₁ into Bernoulli gives P₁ − P₂ in terms of v₁ and the two areas.

steps.label: Speed formula
lines: Solving for v₁, and taking the square
root:
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. Box the final formula for v₁.
steps.why: This boxed formula is the actual output of the instrument: it converts a pressure reading into a speed.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the square on (A₁/A₂) inside the bracket.
Writing v₂ instead of v₁ on the left of the formula.

recall.must_convey: That v₁ equals the square root of 2(P₁ − P₂) divided by rho times ((A₁/A₂) squared minus 1).

steps.label: Reading the manometer
lines: A manometer is connected between the
wide section and the throat.
The difference in liquid level between
its two arms gives the value of P₁ − P₂
directly.
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. Say the manometer's level difference gives P₁ − P₂ directly.
steps.why: The boxed formula needs a value for P₁ − P₂ from somewhere. This step is where that number actually comes from, in the working instrument.
common_mistakes: Saying the manometer measures the speed directly, rather than the pressure difference.
Leaving out where the manometer is connected, the wide section and the throat.

recall.must_convey: That a manometer connected between the wide section and the throat gives P₁ − P₂ from the difference in its liquid levels.

steps.label: Uses
lines: A Venturi meter is used to measure the
speed and flow rate of a fluid moving
through a pipe.
The same principle, a narrow throat
giving higher speed and lower pressure,
is also used in devices such as the
carburettor and the spray gun.
steps.margin_note: Eighth mark. Name flow-rate measurement, and at least one other device using the same principle.
steps.why: Naming a use is what shows the formula is not just an algebra result, it is why the instrument is built at all.
common_mistakes: Naming a device that does not use a narrow throat, such as a plain pressure gauge.
Stopping at flow-rate measurement without naming a second device.

recall.must_convey: That a Venturi meter measures the speed or flow rate of a fluid in a pipe, and that the same narrow-throat principle is used in the carburettor and the spray gun.
